newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: First S.African offshore diamond ship commissioned.
newsitem.headline: First S.African offshore diamond ship commissioned.

text.p: South Africa's first floating diamond mine was commissioned in Cape Town on Thursday and is due to start mining off the country's west coast in early 1997.
The 85-metre, $10 million vessel Moonstar was officially commissioned by Mineral and Energy Affairs Minister Penuell Maduna and will undergo sea trials before starting work.

A joint venture between Benguela Concessions Ltd (Benco) and Moonstone Diamond Corporation NL, Moonstar is expected to mine up to 325,000 carats over five years at an average rate of 65,000 carats a year.
It will mine two blocks in the B prospecting zone, which is four kilometres wide and one kilometre off the west coast and south of the Orange River next to Namaqualand.
The Moonstar has a processing capacity of about 50 tonnes an hour and can stay at sea for up to 21 days, operating continuously, with staff being ferried on and off by helicopter.
The 2,350 tonne ship is equipped with two 20 inch airlift mining heads which suck sediment at a maximum rate of 400 tonnes an hour.

It also has a state-of-the-art position fixing system to ensure comprehensive sea floor cleaning, and a 50 tonne per hour concentrating plant that processes the sediment and an X-ray diamond sorter. Diamonds will be airlifted as and when volumes dictate.

The diamonds to be mined are 95 percent gemstones and "we expect to find diamonds of between 0.3 and 0.4 carats in average size and we would expect that the biggest diamond we will find will be about 20 carats," Benco chairman John Gurney said.
He said there would be "a high proportion of whites (diamonds) and a fair proportion of yellows."
Moonstone chairman Yannic Mercier said that his company had decided 18 months ago to concentrate the bulk of its funds into projects that were likely to result in cash flow.
After considering several countries, Moonstone settled on South Africa 10 months ago.
The venture is expected to make a significant difference to Benco's bottom line, which, as an exploration company, has been consistently in the red for several years.

Mercier said that the gross annual income of the joint venture could, "on the conservative side", be US$10 million a year leaving a pre-tax profit of between $4 million and $5.5 million a year after operating expenses.
For the year ended May 1995, Benco recorded sales of about seven million rand and a loss of 5.7 million rand.
Profits would be split 50-50 but Moonstone would get 7.5 percent extra until the ship had been paid off, while Benco would get four percent extra for management fees.
Once the ship has been paid off, Moonstone's initial share in the venture would be reduced to between two and four percent, depending on production rates.
Benco markets its diamonds by sealed tender to selected buyers, Gurney said.
